Data Vault vs Kimball

One electricity-retailer example, modeled two different ways. The same Customer–Contract domain shows why Data Vault is strong for integration and traceability, while Kimball is strong for reporting and analytics.

CustomerContractElectricity Retail Historical TrackingPower BI Reporting

The simplest way to think about them

Data Vault asks: “What arrived, from which source, how are business entities related, and how did that information change?”
Kimball asks: “How should the business analyze customers, contracts, products, consumption and revenue?”

Source Systems / CRM
→
Data Vault
→
Kimball Data Mart
→

They are not necessarily competitors. A common enterprise pattern is to use Data Vault as the integration/history layer and publish business-friendly Kimball star schemas above it.

1. Data Vault — Customer & Contract

How it models the domain

  • Hub: stable business identities — Customer and Contract.
  • Link: the relationship — which Customer is associated with which Contract.
  • Satellite: descriptive and time-varying attributes, grouped by source, subject or rate of change.
  • New history is generally appended rather than overwriting the past.

What it optimizes for

  • Multi-source integration.
  • Auditability and lineage.
  • Full historical tracking.
  • Resilience when source systems and attributes change.
  • Separating business keys/relationships from descriptive context.
Data Vault example: Customer Hub + Contract Hub + Customer–Contract Link, with multiple Satellites.

2. Kimball — the same Customer & Contract domain

How it models the domain

  • Dimensions: Customer, Contract, Product, Site and Date describe the business context.
  • Facts: Consumption, billing, sales, churn or snapshots capture measurable business events.
  • Surrogate keys connect facts to dimensions.
  • SCD Type 2 can preserve important dimension history.

What it optimizes for

  • Simple and intuitive business reporting.
  • Fast aggregation and BI queries.
  • Clear measures and dimensions.
  • Power BI / Tableau / semantic-model consumption.
  • Business questions such as customers by product, revenue by month and consumption by state.
Kimball example: a star schema centered on FACT_CONSUMPTION with business-friendly dimensions.

Same business question, very different experience

Suppose the business asks: “How many active SSO contracts do we have by state, and what is their monthly consumption?”

Directly from Data Vault

You may need to resolve the latest relevant Customer and Contract Satellites, traverse the Customer–Contract Link, join product/site information and then derive the analytical state as of the reporting date.

H_CUSTOMER + S_CUSTOMER_* + L_CUSTOMER_CONTRACT + H_CONTRACT + S_CONTRACT_* + product/site structures → business logic
→

From Kimball

The difficult integration logic has already been resolved. The report works with dimensions and a fact at a defined grain.

FACT_CONSUMPTION + DIM_CONTRACT + DIM_PRODUCT + DIM_SITE + DIM_DATE → Power BI

Advantages and trade-offs

Data Vault

Advantages: strong traceability, flexible source onboarding, excellent history, clear separation of identities/relationships/attributes, suitable for regulated and complex data estates.

Trade-offs: more tables, more joins, steeper learning curve, greater engineering overhead, and usually needs an additional serving layer for analysts.

Kimball

Advantages: easy for analysts, excellent for BI, intuitive business vocabulary, efficient aggregation, clear grain and metrics.

Trade-offs: integration and lineage are less intrinsic; changing sources or business definitions can require remodeling; history must be intentionally designed.

Which one should you use?

SituationBetter fitWhy
Several operational systems feed the warehouseData VaultSeparates business identities, relationships, source-specific attributes and history.
Migration from a legacy platform to a new platformData VaultUseful when old and new representations differ and traceability matters.
Regulatory/audit requirement to reconstruct historical dataData VaultHistorical lineage is a first-class concern.
Power BI dashboards and analyst self-serviceKimballStar schemas are substantially easier to consume.
Consumption, revenue, sales, churn and billable reportingKimballFacts and dimensions map naturally to analytical questions.
Large enterprise with both needsData Vault + KimballVault handles integration/history; Kimball becomes the reporting/data-mart layer.
Practical takeaway: Data Vault is usually closer to the engineering/integration side of the warehouse; Kimball is closer to the analytics/semantic/reporting side. In a mature architecture, the two can complement each other rather than forcing a single modeling technique everywhere.

Databricks orchestration — recommended design

For this architecture, the cleanest separation of responsibilities is: Lakeflow Jobs orchestrates the workflow; dbt owns SQL transformation dependencies; Lakeflow/Auto Loader handles ingestion where appropriate; Unity Catalog governs the data.

Recommended pattern: do not create one Databricks task for every Hub, Link, Satellite, Dimension and Fact. Let dbt's DAG resolve model-level dependencies through ref(), while Lakeflow Jobs orchestrates larger stages, schedules, retries, notifications and non-dbt work.

Lakeflow Jobs — macro orchestration

  • Schedule or event trigger.
  • Coordinate ingestion, dbt, validation and downstream refresh tasks.
  • Task-level dependencies and conditional paths.
  • Retries, timeout policies and failure notifications.
  • Operational monitoring of the end-to-end run.

dbt — transformation orchestration

  • Model dependencies through ref().
  • Build Hub / Link / Satellite patterns and downstream marts.
  • Tests, documentation and model lineage.
  • Incremental materializations where appropriate.
  • Selectors/tags can run only the required domain or layer.

A practical electricity-retailer workflow

Lakeflow Job: daily_customer_contract_pipeline Task 1 ingest_source_systems ↓ Task 2 ingestion_quality_gate ↓ Task 3 dbt_build_data_vault ├─ stg_customer ├─ stg_contract ├─ h_customer ├─ h_contract ├─ l_customer_contract ├─ s_customer_details └─ s_contract_details ↓ Task 4 dbt_build_marts ├─ dim_customer ├─ dim_contract ├─ dim_product ├─ fact_billable_snapshot └─ fact_consumption ↓ Task 5 reporting_quality_gate ↓ Task 6 semantic / Power BI downstream step

Inside Tasks 3 and 4, dbt determines the detailed table execution order. This keeps the Lakeflow Job understandable even when the Data Vault grows to hundreds of tables.

Why not orchestrate every Data Vault table manually?

ApproachWhat happensAssessment
One Databricks task per tableThe workflow DAG can become enormous as Hub, Link and Satellite counts grow. Dependency changes require orchestration changes.Avoid for large Data Vault implementations
One giant notebookEasy initially, but transformation logic, testing and lineage become coupled and harder to maintain.Useful for prototypes, weak long-term boundary
Lakeflow Jobs + dbtLakeflow controls the end-to-end workflow while dbt controls SQL-model dependencies.Recommended default for SQL-heavy Vault + marts
Lakeflow Jobs + Lakeflow pipelines + dbtPipeline technology handles ingestion/streaming tables; dbt handles analytical transformations; Jobs coordinates both.Strong option for a broader Databricks-native platform
External Airflow + DatabricksAn external orchestrator coordinates Databricks plus many non-Databricks platforms.Consider when orchestration genuinely spans a wider enterprise ecosystem

Suggested layer and repository structure

Databricks / Unity Catalog

catalog ├── bronze │ ├── source_system_a_* │ └── source_system_b_* ├── vault │ ├── h_* │ ├── l_* │ └── s_* └── gold ├── dim_* └── fact_*

dbt project

models/ ├── staging/ │ ├── source_system_a/ │ └── source_system_b/ ├── vault/ │ ├── hubs/ │ ├── links/ │ └── satellites/ └── marts/ ├── dimensions/ └── facts/

Keep the code in Git and deploy production jobs consistently. For Data Vault specifically, reusable macros or metadata-driven generation can reduce repetitive Hub/Link/Satellite SQL, but generated models should still be testable, documented and version-controlled.
